cards.heading: Why nginx holds thousands of idle connections cheaply
cards.hook: Apache spawns a thread per connection; nginx runs one event loop per worker on epoll/kqueue, so an idle keep-alive connection costs almost nothing while it waits.
cards.body: One worker can comfortably hold tens of thousands of idle sockets at once because there's no thread sitting around for each of them.

cards.heading: The master process never touches client traffic
cards.hook: The master only reads config, opens listening sockets, and spawns workers — actual requests are handled entirely by workers, so a crashed worker gets replaced without the master itself ever going down.

cards.heading: Workers drop root immediately after binding
cards.hook: The master runs as root just long enough to bind privileged ports 80/443, then forks workers that drop to an unprivileged user before parsing a single byte of untrusted client input.
cards.body: If you ever see nginx processes all running as root, that's a misconfiguration, not a quirk.

cards.heading: worker_connections is a hard ceiling, and it's halved for a proxy
cards.hook: worker_connections 1024 with 4 workers means 4096 total connections, full stop — and as a reverse proxy, one client request occupies two of those slots at once, client-facing and backend-facing.
cards.body: Real client capacity is roughly half the raw number as a result — a common sizing mistake.

cards.heading: multi_accept isn't a free win
cards.hook: Letting a worker grab every pending connection in one pass sounds strictly better, but under very high connection churn it can let one worker hog new connections and briefly starve its own request processing.
cards.body: Nginx leaves it off by default on purpose — benchmark before enabling it.

cards.heading: sendfile, tcp_nopush, and tcp_nodelay work as a trio
cards.hook: sendfile skips copying a file into nginx's own buffer, tcp_nopush holds packets until they're full, and tcp_nodelay flushes the final small packet immediately instead of waiting up to 200ms on Nagle's algorithm.
cards.body: All three are conventionally turned on together rather than treated as alternatives.

cards.heading: add_header silently skips error responses without always
cards.hook: Without the always keyword, add_header is dropped for anything that isn't a 2xx or 3xx response — meaning your security headers quietly vanish exactly on the error pages where you'd want them most.

cards.heading: Location matching isn't longest-match or first-match uniformly
cards.hook: Nginx checks prefix locations for the longest match first, lets an exact match or a ^~ prefix win instantly, and only falls through to regex locations — checked in file order, first match wins — if neither shortcut fired.
cards.body: A later, more specific regex can still lose to an earlier, broader one purely because of where it sits in the file.

cards.heading: ^~ is the escape hatch from regex locations
cards.hook: Marking a prefix location with ^~ tells nginx to stop and use it immediately once it's the longest prefix match, skipping regex checking entirely — the standard way to guarantee a static-asset path bypasses a PHP handler regex.

cards.heading: Nginx becomes the client once it proxies
cards.hook: The moment proxy_pass forwards a request, nginx is now a client to your app, not just a server to the browser — which is why X-Real-IP and X-Forwarded-For have to be set explicitly, or your app's logs only ever see nginx's own IP.

cards.heading: X-Forwarded-Proto tells the app about TLS it can't see itself
cards.hook: The nginx-to-backend hop is commonly plain HTTP even when the public side is HTTPS — without X-Forwarded-Proto, an app behind an SSL-terminating proxy can't tell it's being accessed securely, breaking redirect-to-HTTPS logic into a loop.

cards.heading: Three different proxy timeouts, three different failures
cards.hook: proxy_connect_timeout is the TCP handshake, proxy_send_timeout is writing the request, proxy_read_timeout is waiting for the response.
cards.body: A slow database query shows up specifically as a read timeout, not a connect one, and that distinction tells you where to actually look.

cards.heading: proxy_buffering decouples a slow client from a fast backend
cards.hook: With buffering on, nginx reads the whole upstream response into its own buffers so the backend can move on immediately, while nginx separately handles trickling bytes out to a slow client.

cards.heading: An HTTP/1.0 default silently breaks WebSocket upgrades
cards.hook: Nginx defaults to speaking HTTP/1.0 to upstreams, which has no Upgrade mechanism at all — proxy_http_version 1.1 is required before a WebSocket handshake can ever succeed.

cards.heading: A healthy idle WebSocket looks exactly like a stalled request
cards.hook: The default 60-second read/send timeouts will silently kill a perfectly healthy but quiet WebSocket — chat apps stretch these to 86400 seconds specifically because idle time is normal, not a failure.

cards.heading: Round robin is fair by count, not by cost
cards.hook: With no load-balancing directive set, nginx just cycles through servers in order — fair per request, but if one request type is far more expensive than another, round robin can still pile uneven work onto one backend by bad luck.

cards.heading: least_conn adapts to uneven request duration
cards.hook: Sending each request to whichever backend has the fewest active connections right now means a backend stuck on a few slow requests naturally gets fewer new ones until it frees up — round robin can't see that at all.

cards.heading: ip_hash trades flexibility for free session affinity
cards.hook: Hashing the client IP routes the same client to the same backend every time with no shared session store needed — but if a backend goes down, the whole hash distribution shifts, rebalancing even unaffected clients onto a different server.

cards.heading: backup servers take zero traffic until everything else fails
cards.hook: A server marked backup gets nothing under normal conditions — it only activates once every non-backup server is marked unavailable, existing purely as a last resort, not extra capacity.

cards.heading: Passive health checks only learn from real traffic
cards.hook: max_fails and fail_timeout mark a server unavailable only after it actually fails real client requests that many times — there's no independent polling, which is the free open-source mechanism; proactive polling is an Nginx Plus feature.

cards.heading: Upstream keepalive needs two more lines to actually work
cards.hook: Adding keepalive 32 to reuse backend connections does nothing by itself — nginx still defaults to HTTP/1.0 upstream and forwards whatever Connection header the client sent, breaking the pool silently.

cards.heading: HTTP/2 retires a decade of asset-bundling hacks
cards.hook: listen 443 ssl http2 lets many requests share one TCP connection without blocking each other — exactly why bundling JS/CSS and sharding assets across hostnames mattered under HTTP/1.1, and matters far less once HTTP/2 is in play.

cards.heading: Session resumption cache is shared across workers, not across machines
cards.hook: ssl_session_cache shared:SSL:10m lets a returning client skip the full TLS handshake — but that cache is shared only across one instance's workers, so a fleet behind a load balancer needs its own cross-node resumption mechanism.

cards.heading: OCSP stapling removes a round trip and a privacy leak
cards.hook: Without stapling, a client checks certificate revocation by contacting the CA itself during the handshake — slow, and it tells the CA which site that client is visiting. Stapling has nginx fetch and staple that proof onto the handshake directly.

cards.heading: HSTS is a one-way door
cards.hook: Once a browser caches Strict-Transport-Security, it refuses plain HTTP to that host entirely until max-age expires, errors and all — don't ship a long max-age until HTTPS is confirmed stable across every subdomain.

cards.heading: Let's Encrypt's challenge path has to dodge your own redirect
cards.hook: The ACME http-01 challenge is served over plain HTTP at /.well-known/acme-challenge/ — if that path gets swept into a blanket redirect-to-HTTPS, certificate issuance and every automated renewal silently fail.

cards.heading: Session tickets can undermine the forward secrecy you just configured
cards.hook: Forward-secret ciphers mean a leaked private key can't decrypt old traffic — but a session ticket key isn't rotated as carefully, and compromising it can retroactively expose every session it resumed.
cards.body: That's why ssl_session_tickets off, relying solely on the shared session cache, is the more conservative choice.

cards.heading: Negative caching stops a flood over a resource that doesn't exist
cards.hook: Caching 404 responses for a short duration, separately from 200s, stops repeated requests for a genuinely missing resource from hammering the backend on every single try.

cards.heading: Stale-while-revalidate trades perfect freshness for uptime
cards.hook: proxy_cache_use_stale serves a previously cached copy if the upstream errors, times out, or is mid-refresh — almost always the right trade for anything that isn't financial or security-sensitive data.

cards.heading: Cache lock stops a stampede on cold URLs
cards.hook: When many requests arrive at once for something not yet cached, proxy_cache_lock sends only the first one to the upstream and makes the rest wait briefly, instead of all of them hitting the backend simultaneously.

cards.heading: immutable caching only makes sense with cache-busted filenames
cards.hook: Cache-Control: immutable tells the browser never to even revalidate on reload — safe for a year-long cache only if the filename changes whenever the content does.
cards.body: Using it on a URL that can change in place serves stale content to returning visitors indefinitely.

cards.heading: Nginx's rate limiter is a leaky bucket, not a fixed window
cards.hook: rate=10r/s really means one request drains every 100ms on average — understanding that model is what makes burst and nodelay make sense instead of feeling like arbitrary numbers.

cards.heading: burst without nodelay silently delays requests instead of rejecting them
cards.hook: Without nodelay, requests inside the burst allowance get queued and smoothed out rather than rejected — often a worse experience than either serving immediately or failing clearly.

cards.heading: 429 is the honest status code for a rate limit
cards.hook: Nginx's own default rate-limit rejection is 503, which misleadingly implies the service is down — setting limit_req_status 429 tells well-behaved clients to back off and retry, which is what actually happened.

cards.heading: allow/deny is evaluated top to bottom, first match wins
cards.hook: Put deny all before your allow rules by mistake and every request hits the deny first — the allow lines become unreachable dead code. Specific allows first, catch-all deny last, is the only order that works.

cards.heading: CSP's real protection requires giving up unsafe-inline
cards.hook: default-src 'self' without unsafe-inline or unsafe-eval is a genuinely restrictive starting point — adding those keywords back in reopens most of the injection vectors Content-Security-Policy exists to close.

cards.heading: Slowloris defenses bound time between bytes, not total request time
cards.hook: client_body_timeout and client_header_timeout stop an attacker sending a legitimate-looking request one byte at a time to exhaust every worker connection slot — they bound the wait for the next chunk, not the whole request's duration.

cards.heading: An SPA needs a different try_files ending than a static site
cards.hook: A static site's try_files ends in =404; a single-page app's ends in /index.html instead, so a client-side router can take over rendering any deep-linked route that has no real file on disk.
cards.body: The tradeoff: nginx's own logs can no longer tell a valid client-side route from a typo'd one — both return 200.

cards.heading: depends_on only orders container startup, not readiness
cards.hook: Docker Compose's depends_on starts nginx after the app container, but nginx can bind its port before the app is actually accepting connections — producing a brief window of 502s, not a readiness guarantee.

cards.heading: Four timing variables turn a log line into a diagnosis
cards.hook: request_time, upstream_connect_time, upstream_header_time, and upstream_response_time each isolate a different phase of a request.
cards.body: A high header time with a low connect time points at backend processing speed; the reverse points at network or connection issues — all from the log line alone.

cards.heading: nginx -s reload is why config changes don't drop connections
cards.hook: Reload spawns a fresh set of workers on the new config and lets old workers finish in-flight requests before exiting — a restart would drop every open connection immediately instead.
cards.body: Always run nginx -t first: a broken config fails the reload safely, but only if you catch the typo before, not after.

cards.heading: A gateway is a reverse proxy plus every per-service repeated concern
cards.hook: Auth, per-client rate limits, a consistent error format, tracing, and CORS — a gateway implements these once at the edge instead of duplicated, or forgotten, in every backend service behind it.

cards.heading: rewrite strips the public prefix before the backend ever sees it
cards.hook: A backend service rarely knows or cares what public path it's mounted under — rewriting the prefix away lets the gateway own the public URL shape while the service keeps its own internal one.
cards.code:
proxy_pass http://user_service/;
# trailing slash on both sides strips the prefix without an explicit rewrite

cards.heading: auth_request delegates the allow/deny decision to a subrequest
cards.hook: Before proxying the real request, nginx fires an internal subrequest to a validation endpoint and waits — a 2xx lets the real request through, a 401 or 403 returns to the client immediately and the backend never sees it at all.

cards.heading: internal; stops a client from hitting your auth endpoint directly
cards.hook: Marking the validation location internal means it only ever answers subrequests nginx generates itself — never a request that arrived straight from outside.

cards.heading: Stock nginx has no built-in JWT verification
cards.hook: Verifying a signature and reading claims is logic, not configuration — the realistic options are delegating to a small service via auth_request, using njs to decode it inline, or Nginx Plus's commercial auth_jwt directive.

cards.heading: mTLS gives service-to-service traffic an unforgeable identity
cards.hook: ssl_verify_client on plus a trusted CA rejects any connection without a properly signed client certificate, and the verified certificate subject is a strong identity cryptographically tied to the handshake — not a header a caller could fake.

cards.heading: A B2B API should rate limit by API key, not IP
cards.hook: Keying the limit zone on the client's IP is wrong for an API gateway — many legitimate customers share one corporate NAT IP, and one customer might call from many IPs that should still share one fair-use quota.

cards.heading: A built-in request ID threads one identifier through every hop
cards.hook: $request_id generates a unique ID per request with no module needed — forward it to the backend and return it to the client, and a user reporting a bug can hand you the exact ID to search for instead of a timestamp.

cards.heading: proxy_hide_header stops internal details leaking to API consumers
cards.hook: A backend's internal diagnostic headers — a service version, an internal hostname — are useful between your own services but shouldn't reach an external caller; proxy_hide_header strips them before the response leaves the gateway.

cards.heading: Handling the preflight once means no backend needs its own CORS logic
cards.hook: A browser's OPTIONS preflight expects a fast, bodyless answer — answering it centrally at the gateway means every service behind it inherits the same CORS policy without implementing or agreeing on one itself.

cards.heading: proxy_intercept_errors normalizes failures the backend never answered
cards.hook: Different teams' backends return wildly inconsistent error bodies — HTML, a bare string, three different JSON shapes. Intercepting 5xx and substituting one consistent JSON contract fixes that for every failure mode the gateway can see.

cards.heading: Path-based versioning is debuggable, header-based is invisible unless logged
cards.hook: /v1/ versus /v2/ shows the version in every log line and bug report; header-based content negotiation keeps URLs stable across versions but silently disappears from access logs unless explicitly added to the log format.

cards.heading: Nginx proxies gRPC natively, but errors need special handling
cards.hook: grpc_pass speaks gRPC's HTTP/2 wire protocol directly — but when nginx itself generates an error, it wants to return a plain HTTP 502, while a gRPC client expects a grpc-status trailer instead.

cards.heading: Structured JSON logs are what make a gateway's logs queryable
cards.hook: A gateway sees every API call across every backend — logging it in nginx's classic space-delimited format wastes that advantage; a JSON log format lets any aggregation system ingest it without a fragile parsing regex.

cards.heading: Nginx isn't a developer portal, schema validator, or plugin marketplace
cards.hook: A dedicated gateway like Kong or Apigee adds API catalogs, OpenAPI-based request validation, and a plugin ecosystem — nginx's honest answer to all three is write it yourself in njs or delegate to a service.
cards.body: Kong itself is built on OpenResty, nginx core plus Lua — reaching for a dedicated gateway is nginx with those gaps pre-filled, not an alternative to it.

cards.heading: Nginx's default buffering is exactly wrong for real-time delivery
cards.hook: Buffering the whole upstream response before forwarding it is the right default for an ordinary API call — it's exactly what breaks a WebSocket, an SSE stream, or a live video feed, each needing bytes to flow immediately.

cards.heading: A map variable makes the Upgrade header safe to forward conditionally
cards.hook: Hardcoding Connection: upgrade breaks the moment the same path ever serves an ordinary HTTP request too — a map on the Upgrade header forwards upgrade only when the client actually asked for one.

cards.heading: ip_hash pins a socket to the backend holding its state
cards.hook: A WebSocket connection has no per-request re-routing once it's open — ip_hash keeps a client on the same backend across reconnects, which matters only if that backend holds in-memory state about the connection.
cards.body: The real fix at scale is a shared pub/sub layer that decouples who holds the socket from who knows about the message — then plain least_conn works fine.

cards.heading: Nginx has no idea what a ping/pong frame is
cards.hook: To nginx, an upgraded WebSocket is just an opaque TCP byte stream — proxy_read_timeout only fires when nothing crosses the wire at all, so heartbeats have to be the application's job, on a shorter interval than nginx's own timeout.

cards.heading: proxy_buffering off is the one setting that makes SSE work
cards.hook: With buffering on, nginx waits for its buffers to fill or the backend to finish before forwarding anything — for a stream that's intentionally never-ending, the client waits indefinitely for data already sitting on the server.

cards.heading: gzip has the same conflict with streaming that buffering does
cards.hook: Compression wants to accumulate enough output to compress efficiently before writing anything — turning gzip off for a streaming location removes exactly the delay disabling proxy_buffering was meant to fix.

cards.heading: X-Accel-Buffering lets the application decide per response
cards.hook: When the same path sometimes streams and sometimes doesn't, the app can set X-Accel-Buffering: no on just that response instead of needing a dedicated location block.

cards.heading: A comment line keeps SSE alive through hops nginx doesn't control
cards.hook: A periodic keep-alive comment is valid SSE syntax the EventSource API silently ignores — it exists to defeat idle-connection timeouts on corporate proxies and load balancers between client and server, which nginx's own timeout can't reach.

cards.heading: Faststart encoding is what makes seeking before a full download possible
cards.hook: An MP4's moov atom, the index of where every frame lives, has to sit at the front of the file, not the end, or a player has to download the whole thing before it can calculate where frame N is.

cards.heading: Nginx's mp4 module recalculates byte ranges for a seek request
cards.hook: When a player asks to start at a given second, the mp4 module uses the faststart-indexed moov atom to work out exactly which frames to serve from that point forward, instead of streaming from byte zero.

cards.heading: Manifest and segment files need opposite caching rules
cards.hook: A live .m3u8 manifest is rewritten every few seconds — caching it even briefly leaves players stuck on a stale segment list. A .ts segment, once written, never changes, so it's safe to cache for a year as immutable.
cards.body: Getting this backwards is the single most common HLS misconfiguration, and it shows up as a stream that keeps freezing a few seconds behind live.

cards.heading: CORS silently blocks HLS.js even when the request succeeds
cards.hook: hls.js and dash.js fetch manifests and segments via ordinary fetch or XHR, frequently from a different origin than the media host — without CORS headers, the browser blocks the player from reading a response that actually arrived.

cards.heading: aio plus directio bypasses the page cache for very large files
cards.hook: For files comfortably larger than available RAM, reading them via asynchronous I/O that skips the OS page cache avoids one huge file evicting everything else useful from it.
cards.body: The cost: no page-cache benefit for that file's own repeated reads — worth it only once files are well beyond RAM size.

cards.heading: Chat is wide and shallow, video is narrow and deep
cards.hook: Tens of thousands of mostly-idle chat sockets stress connection count, not bandwidth — a handful of video streams each pulling megabits stress bandwidth and disk throughput, not connection count.
cards.body: Tuning the wrong knob for either wastes the effort entirely.

cards.heading: A proxied connection costs two file descriptors, not one
cards.hook: worker_rlimit_nofile has to clear worker_processes times worker_connections with real headroom, because every proxied connection holds both a client-facing and a backend-facing socket at once.
cards.body: A 50,000-connection chat server needs well over 100,000 file descriptors once the backend-facing half of every proxy is counted.

cards.heading: Scale isn't one number, it's five separate axes
cards.hook: Throughput, concurrent connections, configuration surface area, geographic distribution, and rate of change each stress nginx differently — a chat fleet can be under enormous connection pressure with almost no throughput pressure at all.

cards.heading: Nginx's scaling story is really an idle-connection story
cards.hook: A thread-per-connection server pays a fixed memory and scheduling cost whether or not a connection is doing anything — nginx's event loop does nothing until the kernel says there's real work.
cards.body: That's the entire reason the C10K problem stopped being a serious engineering challenge once nginx and its contemporaries existed.

cards.heading: TLS session cache doesn't share across a fleet by default
cards.hook: The shared session cache is shared across one instance's workers, not across nodes — a client whose session was cached on node A pays for a full handshake again if load-balanced to node B.
cards.body: Fleets fix this by terminating TLS one layer further out, or distributing a shared ticket key across every nginx node.

cards.heading: ingress-nginx is a control loop in front of ordinary location blocks
cards.hook: Every routing rule a Kubernetes cluster generates is still, underneath, the exact same location block from ordinary nginx config — a controller just regenerates and reloads it automatically instead of a human hand-editing nginx.conf.

cards.heading: Nginx scales horizontally by being easy to run many copies of
cards.hook: The actual fleet pattern is many identical, stateless instances behind something else that spreads traffic — nginx contributes almost no special clustering feature to this on its own.

cards.heading: Cloudflare scaled past nginx, not just on it
cards.hook: Cloudflare ran heavily patched nginx at its edge for years, then publicly migrated to Pingora, a Rust proxy built from scratch, once its scale hit a point where nginx's reload model and per-connection memory overhead became the limiting factor.

cards.heading: A CPU-heavy operation on one connection blocks every other on that worker
cards.hook: Nginx's event loop makes idle connections nearly free, but a slow regex or an expensive Lua script makes the opposite mistake costly — since each worker is single-threaded, it blocks everything else that worker holds for as long as it runs.

cards.heading: nginx -s reload assumes config changes slowly
cards.hook: Reload is elegant for a few deploys a day — it was never built for routing decisions that need to change thousands of times a second, which is precisely the gap Envoy's dynamic configuration API was built to fill for service meshes.

cards.heading: Dynamic upstream membership isn't native to open-source nginx
cards.hook: The upstream block is a static list, re-read only on reload — picking up a newly added backend without reloading needs a templating sidecar, DNS-based re-resolution, or Nginx Plus's commercial API.

cards.heading: Round robin is simple and fair only when servers are identical
cards.hook: Cycling through servers in a fixed order works great when every backend has equal capacity and similar request costs — a mixed-capacity fleet or uneven request durations expose its blind spot immediately.

cards.heading: Weighted round robin sends traffic proportional to capacity
cards.hook: A server with weight 3 gets three requests for every one a weight-1 server gets — the standard way to send proportionally more load to a bigger instance without needing least-connections' dynamic tracking.
cards.code:
server backend1.example.com weight=3;
server backend2.example.com weight=1;

cards.heading: IP hash breaks down behind a shared NAT
cards.hook: A hundred users behind one corporate NAT IP all hash to the same backend and overload it — IP hash gives free session affinity, but only when each client genuinely has its own distinguishable IP.

cards.heading: Random load balancing needs no coordination at all
cards.hook: Picking a server at random has no state to track and no shared memory needed across balancer instances — good distribution shows up over large volumes, even though any single short window can look uneven.

cards.heading: Least connections assumes equal capacity and duration
cards.hook: Routing to whichever server has the fewest active connections adapts to varying request length far better than round robin — but it still assumes every connection is roughly equally expensive, which a mix of cheap and heavy requests can violate.

cards.heading: Weighted least connections divides load by both count and capacity
cards.hook: Scoring each server as active connections divided by its weight picks the server with the most spare proportional capacity — the practical answer for a cloud fleet mixing different instance sizes.

cards.heading: Least response time optimizes for what the user actually feels
cards.hook: Tracking a rolling average response time per server and routing new requests to the fastest one catches a server quietly degrading before it ever fails a health check outright.
cards.body: The cost is needing continuous timing data, not just a connection count.

cards.heading: Resource-based balancing needs its own monitoring pipeline
cards.hook: Routing by actual CPU and memory usage is the most accurate load signal possible, but it only works if metrics are being polled and kept fresh — stale metrics are worse than no resource-awareness at all.

cards.heading: Sticky sessions are a workaround for stateful backends
cards.hook: A cookie or IP-based sticky session keeps a client on the same server, which only matters because that server is holding session state locally — the state itself, not the routing, is the actual design decision worth revisiting.

cards.heading: Consistent hashing survives adding or removing servers gracefully
cards.hook: A plain hash-mod-N remaps almost every key when N changes; consistent hashing with virtual nodes on a ring only remaps the keys that belonged to the server actually added or removed.

cards.heading: Active health checks need consecutive successes before trusting a server again
cards.hook: Requiring several consecutive passing checks, not just one, before marking a recovering server healthy again stops a flaky backend from flapping in and out of the pool on a single lucky response.

cards.heading: Passive health checks track an error rate over a rolling window
cards.hook: Instead of a dedicated health endpoint, passive checks watch the real error rate of actual traffic over a time window and only mark a server unhealthy once a minimum request count and an error-rate threshold are both crossed.

cards.heading: Priority-based routing formalizes backup servers into tiers
cards.hook: Instead of one flat pool with a single backup flag, ordering whole server groups by priority lets traffic fail over through several tiers in sequence — primary, secondary, last-resort — each used only once every tier above it is unhealthy.

cards.heading: Geographic load balancing optimizes for latency, not load
cards.hook: Routing a client to the nearest region by calculated distance minimizes network latency — a genuinely different goal from least connections or round robin, which only care about load inside a single region.

cards.heading: Adaptive balancing blends response time and success rate into one score
cards.hook: Scoring each server on a weighted mix of recent response time and success rate, then picking probabilistically rather than deterministically, avoids the pile-on effect a hard cutoff like always pick the single best server would create.

cards.heading: AWS's Layer 7 and Layer 4 balancers solve different problems
cards.hook: An Application Load Balancer routes by path and host at the HTTP layer; a Network Load Balancer hashes source and destination IP and port at the TCP layer for ultra-low latency and a static IP.
cards.body: Picking the wrong one for the job costs you the other one's actual advantage.

cards.heading: Kubernetes Service load balancing happens below your app entirely
cards.hook: A Service of type LoadBalancer round-robins across pod endpoints using iptables or IPVS rules the kernel enforces — sessionAffinity ClientIP is the built-in equivalent of nginx's ip_hash, set declaratively instead of in a config file.

cards.heading: Start with round robin, add complexity only when it's earned
cards.hook: Every dynamic algorithm — least connections, response time, resource-based — trades simplicity and zero overhead for better adaptation to real conditions. The right starting point for most stateless services is still the simplest one.

cards.heading: The right algorithm follows from the constraint, not a love of complexity
cards.hook: Session-based apps want IP hash or sticky sessions, long-lived connections want least connections, multi-region deployments want geographic routing, auto-scaling fleets want weighted least connections.
